units.P2_June2019_Q1|-|text: Given $2^x \times 4^y = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$, express $y$ as a function of $x$. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q1|-|ms: B1: Writes a correct equation in powers of $2$ only, e.g. $2^x \times 2^{2y} = 2^{-3/2}$ (or an equivalent equation using logarithms, e.g. $x\log 2 + 2y\log 2 = \log\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$). M1: Complete process of using correct index laws (or log laws) on a correct equation to obtain $y$ written as a function of $x$. A1: $y = -\frac{x}{2} - \frac{3}{4}$ (o.e., e.g. $y = -\frac{1}{4}(2x+3)$). (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q2|stem:
The speed of a small jet aircraft was measured every $5$ seconds, starting from the time it turned onto a runway, until the time when it left the ground. The results are given in the table below with the time in seconds and the speed in m/s.
Time (s): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25
Speed (m/s): 2, 5, 10, 18, 28, 42
Using all of this information,
units.P2_June2019_Q2|a|text: (a) estimate the length of runway used by the jet to take off. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q2|a|ms: (a) M1: Uses an allowable method to estimate the area under the speed-time curve (e.g. the trapezium rule, a uniform-acceleration equation, or summing rectangles). M1: Correct trapezium rule method with $h=5$ (condone a slip on one of the speeds): $\text{Area} = \frac{5}{2}[2 + 42 + 2(5+10+18+28)]$. A1: $415$ (m) (units not required, but final A0 if incorrect units are given). (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q2|b|text:
Given that the jet accelerated smoothly in these $25$ seconds,
(b) explain whether your answer to part (a) is an underestimate or an overestimate of the length of runway used by the jet to take off. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q2|b|ms: (b) B1ft: Overestimate, with a relevant explanation, e.g. the top of the trapezia lie above the curve / the curve is convex / the acceleration (gradient) is continually increasing, so the area of the trapezia is greater than the area under the curve. (Depends on having obtained an answer to (a) using a trapezium-rule-type method; if a 'sum of rectangles lying below the curve' method was used instead in (a), then 'underestimate' with the explanation 'all the rectangles lie below the curve' is accepted.) (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q3|stem:
Figure 1 shows a sector $AOB$ of a circle with centre $O$, radius $5$ cm and angle $AOB = 40^\circ$. The attempt of a student to find the area of the sector is shown below.
$\text{Area of sector} = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta = \frac{1}{2} \times 5^2 \times 40 = 500 \text{ cm}^2$
units.P2_June2019_Q3|a|text: (a) Explain the error made by this student. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q3|a|ms: (a) B1: Explains that the sector-area formula $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$ is only valid when $\theta$ is measured in radians; the student has substituted $\theta = 40$ in degrees instead of converting to radians. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q3|b|text: (b) Write out a correct solution. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q3|b|ms: (b) M1: Correct application of the sector-area formula using $\theta$ converted to radians ($\theta = \frac{40\pi}{180} = \frac{2\pi}{9}$), or equivalently using the degrees version of the formula, $\frac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2$. A1: $\text{Area} = \frac{25\pi}{9} \text{ cm}^2$, or awrt $8.73 \text{ cm}^2$ (units may be ignored for this mark). (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q4|-|text: Figure 2 shows a sketch of the curve $C_1$ with parametric equations $x = 10\cos t, \; y = 4\sqrt{2}\sin t, \; 0 \leqslant t < 2\pi$, which meets the circle $C_2$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 66$ at four distinct points, as shown in Figure 2. Given that one of these points, $S$, lies in the 4th quadrant, find the Cartesian coordinates of $S$. (6 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q4|-|ms: M1: Begins to solve the problem by applying a complete strategy, e.g. substituting the parametric equations for $C_1$ into the Cartesian equation for $C_2$ to give an equation in one variable ($t$) only (alternative valid strategies: convert $C_1$ to Cartesian form using $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$ and combine with $C_2$; or write $C_2$ in parametric form and combine parametrically). M1: Uses $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$ to reduce the equation to $\sin^2 t$ only, or $\cos^2 t$ only (or, in an $x$/$y$-only approach, to an equation in $x^2$ only or $y^2$ only; or, using double-angle formulae, to an equation in $\cos 2t$ only). A1: Correct resulting equation, e.g. $(10\cos t)^2 + (4\sqrt{2}\sin t)^2 = 66$ leading to $100 - 68\sin^2 t = 66$, i.e. $\sin^2 t = \frac{1}{2}$. dM1: Rearranges to find $\sin t$ (or $\cos t$, or $x^2$/$y^2$, or $\cos 2t$), where the result lies in the valid range; dependent on both previous M marks. M1: Substitutes the solution back into the relevant original equation(s) to obtain the value of the $x$-coordinate and the corresponding $y$-coordinate (note: these may not yet be in the correct quadrant). A1: Selects the coordinates lying in the 4th quadrant: $S = (5\sqrt{2}, -4)$, i.e. $S = ($awrt $7.07, -4)$. (6 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q5|-|text:
Figure 3 shows a sketch of the curve with equation $y = \sqrt{x}$. The point $P(x, y)$ lies on the curve. The rectangle, shown shaded on Figure 3, has height $y$ and width $\delta x$. Calculate
$\lim_{\delta x \to 0} \sum_{x=4}^{9} \sqrt{x}\,\delta x$
(3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q5|-|ms: B1: States that the limit equals the definite integral, $\int_{4}^{9} \sqrt{x} \, dx$ (with or without the '$dx$'). M1: Integrates $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ to give $kx^{3/2}$, $k \neq 0$. A1: Correct value: $\left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}\right]_{4}^{9} = \frac{2}{3} \times 27 - \frac{2}{3} \times 8 = \frac{38}{3}$, i.e. $12$ and $\frac{2}{3}$, or awrt $12.7$. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q6|stem:
Figure 4 shows a sketch of the graph of $y = \mathrm{g}(x)$, where
$\mathrm{g}(x) = (x-2)^2 + 1$, for $x \leqslant 2$
$\mathrm{g}(x) = 4x - 7$, for $x > 2$
units.P2_June2019_Q6|a|ms: (a) M1: Uses a complete method to find $\mathrm{gg}(0)$, e.g. substitutes $x=0$ into $(0-2)^2+1$ to get $5$, then substitutes this result into the relevant branch of g. A1: $\mathrm{gg}(0) = \mathrm{g}(5) = 4(5)-7 = 13$. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q6|b|text: (b) Find all values of $x$ for which $\mathrm{g}(x) > 28$. (4 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q6|b|ms: (b) M1: Solves $(x-2)^2+1 = 28$ (or $4x-7 = 28$) to find a critical value. A1: At least one correct critical value is found: $x = 2 - 3\sqrt{3}$ (awrt $-3.20$) or $x = \frac{35}{4}$ ($= 8.75$). M1: Solves both $(x-2)^2+1 = 28$ [editor: relevant to the branch $x \leqslant 2$] and $4x-7 = 28$ [editor: relevant to the branch $x>2$]. A1: Correct final answer: $x < 2 - 3\sqrt{3}$, $x > \frac{35}{4}$ (i.e. $x > 8.75$) (set notation is acceptable). (4 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q6|c|text:
The function h is defined by
$\mathrm{h}(x) = (x-2)^2 + 1, \; x \leqslant 2$
(c) Explain why h has an inverse but g does not. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q6|c|ms: (c) B1: h is one-one (so has an inverse); g is many-one (so does not have an inverse). A correct explanation conveying both underlined points is needed, e.g. 'h is one-one and g is many-one'. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q6|d|ms: (d) M1: Finds $\mathrm{h}^{-1}(x) = 2 - \sqrt{x-1}$ (or, equivalently, uses the fact that if $\mathrm{h}^{-1}(x) = -\frac{1}{2}$ then $x = \mathrm{h}(-\frac{1}{2})$, without needing $\mathrm{h}^{-1}$ explicitly). M1: Sets $2 - \sqrt{x-1} = -\frac{1}{2}$ (or $x = \mathrm{h}(-\frac{1}{2})$) and attempts to solve for $x$. A1: $x = 7.25$ only, cso. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|stem: A small factory makes bars of soap. On any day, the total cost to the factory, £$y$, of making $x$ bars of soap is modelled to be the sum of two separate elements: a fixed cost, and a cost that is proportional to the number of bars of soap that are made that day.
units.P2_June2019_Q7|a|text: (a) Write down a general equation linking $y$ with $x$, for this model. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|a|ms: (a) B1: $y = kx + c$, where $k > 0$ and $c > 0$ are constants (must be seen in part (a); work here cannot be recovered in (b) or (c)). (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|b|text:
The bars of soap are sold for £2 each. On a day when $800$ bars of soap are made and sold, the factory makes a profit of £500. On a day when $300$ bars of soap are made and sold, the factory makes a loss of £80. Using the above information,
(b) show that $y = 0.84x + 428$ (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|b|ms: (b) M1: Translates the problem into the model by finding the total cost on each day: for $x=800$, $y = 2(800)-500 = 1100$; for $x=300$, $y = 2(300)-(-80) = 680$ [editor: i.e. revenue minus profit, or revenue plus loss]. dM1: Applies the two points $(800,1100)$ and $(300,680)$ to form and solve two simultaneous equations for $k$ and $c$ (e.g. $k = \frac{1100-680}{800-300} = 0.84$, then substitutes back to find $c = 428$). A1*: Correct proof with no errors, leading to $y = 0.84x + 428$ (the answer must be stated in part (b)). (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|c|text: (c) With reference to the model, interpret the significance of the value $0.84$ in the equation. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|c|ms: (c) B1: $0.84$ (in £s) represents the cost of making each extra bar of soap (the direct/marginal cost of making a bar of soap). Do not allow 'profit per bar' or 'selling price per bar'. (1 mark)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|d|text:
Assuming that each bar of soap is sold on the day it is made,
(d) find the least number of bars of soap that must be made on any given day for the factory to make a profit that day. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q7|d|ms: (d) M1: Uses the model, with revenue $2n$ and cost $0.84n+428$, to construct an inequality/equation for profit ($2n > 0.84n + 428$) and rearranges for $n$. A1: $369$ (bars) - the least whole number of bars for which a profit is made (decimal answers not accepted). (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q8|i|ms: (i) M1: Applies $\frac{a}{1-r}$ with their common ratio $r$ (where $-1 < r < 1$) and their value of $a$ (e.g. $a = 20\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = 1.25$). M1: Finds the infinite sum using a completely correct strategy (e.g. sum-to-infinity of the whole series minus the sum of the first three terms, or directly $\frac{a}{1-r}$). A1: $2.5$ (o.e.). (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q8|ii|ms: (ii) Way 1: M1: Some evidence of applying the addition law of logarithms as part of a valid proof, e.g. $\log_5\left(\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{4}{3} \times \cdots \times \frac{50}{49}\right)$. M1: Begins to solve the problem by just writing (or by combining) at least three terms of the sum, including either the first two terms and the last term, or the first term and the last two terms, e.g. $\log_5\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) + \log_5\left(\frac{4}{3}\right) + \cdots + \log_5\left(\frac{50}{49}\right)$. Way 2: M1: Uses the subtraction law of logarithms to give $\log_5\left(\frac{n+2}{n+1}\right) = \log_5(n+2) - \log_5(n+1)$. M1: Writes at least three terms for each of $\log_5(n+2)$ and $\log_5(n+1)$ (first two and last, or first and last two), e.g. $(\log_5 3 + \log_5 4 + \cdots + \log_5 50) - (\log_5 2 + \log_5 3 + \cdots + \log_5 49)$. A1*: Correct proof leading to $\log_5\left(\frac{50}{2}\right) = \log_5 25 = 2$. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q9|stem: A research engineer is testing the effectiveness of the braking system of a car when it is driven in wet conditions. The engineer measures and records the braking distance, $d$ metres, when the brakes are applied from a speed of $V$ km/h. Graphs of $d$ against $V$ and $\log_{10} d$ against $\log_{10} V$ were plotted. Figure 5 shows the graph of $d$ against $V$, with a data point $(30, 20)$ marked on the curve. Figure 6 shows the graph of $\log_{10} d$ against $\log_{10} V$, a straight line with vertical-axis intercept $-1.77$.
units.P2_June2019_Q9|a|text:
(a) Explain how Figure 6 would lead the engineer to believe that the braking distance should be modelled by the formula
$d = kV^n$, where $k$ and $n$ are constants,
with $k \approx 0.017$ (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q9|a|ms: (a) M1: Writes $\log_{10} d = \log_{10} k + n\log_{10} V$ (or $\log_{10} d = m\log_{10} V + c$, or $\log_{10} d = m\log_{10} V - 1.77$), seen or used as part of the argument. A1: Alludes to $d = kV^n$ and gives a full explanation by comparing the result with a linear model $Y = MX + C$ [editor: i.e. a straight-line log-log graph implies a power-law relationship between $d$ and $V$]. B1*: $k = 10^{-1.77} =$ awrt $0.017$, linked together with the $-1.77$ intercept in the same part of the question. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q9|b|text:
Using the information given in Figure 5, with $k = 0.017$,
(b) find a complete equation for the model, giving the value of $n$ to 3 significant figures. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q9|b|ms: (b) M1: Applies $V=30$ and $d=20$ to the model (correct way round), i.e. $20 = k(30)^n$ or $\log_{10} 20 = \log_{10} k + n\log_{10} 30$. M1: Applies $(V,d) = (30,20)$ and applies logarithms correctly, rearranging to find $n$. A1: $n =$ awrt $2.08$, giving $d = 0.017V^{2.08}$ (or $\log_{10} d = -1.77 + 2.08\log_{10} V$). (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q9|c|text:
Sean is driving this car at $60$ km/h in wet conditions when he notices a large puddle in the road $100$ m ahead. It takes him $0.8$ seconds to react before applying the brakes.
(c) Use your formula to find out if Sean will be able to stop before reaching the puddle. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q9|c|ms: (c) M1: Applies $V=60$ to the model to find the braking distance $d$ ($d = 0.017(60)^{2.08}$, awrt $84.9$). M1: Uses the model in a correct problem-solving process, either adding a 'thinking distance' ($0.8 \times$ velocity in m/s $=$ awrt $13.3$ m) to the braking distance to find the total stopping distance, or subtracting the thinking distance from $100$ m and comparing with $d$. A1ft: Correct comparison and conclusion, e.g. $13.3 + 84.9 = 98.25 < 100$, so Sean stops in time (a thinking distance of awrt $13$ and a value of $d$ in the range $[81.5, 88.5]$ are required for A1ft). (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q10|stem: Figure 7 shows a sketch of triangle $OAB$. The point $C$ is such that $\overrightarrow{OC} = 2\overrightarrow{OA}$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. The straight line through $C$ and $M$ cuts $OB$ at the point $N$. Given $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$,
units.P2_June2019_Q10|a|text: (a) Find $\overrightarrow{CM}$ in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q10|a|ms: (a) M1: Valid attempt to find $\overrightarrow{CM}$ using a combination of the known vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, e.g. $\overrightarrow{CM} = \overrightarrow{CA} + \overrightarrow{AM} = -\mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})$, or $\overrightarrow{CM} = \overrightarrow{CB} + \overrightarrow{BM} = (-2\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}) + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b})$. A1: Correct simplified answer: $\overrightarrow{CM} = -\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}$. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q10|b|text: (b) Show that $\overrightarrow{ON} = \left(2 - \frac{3}{2}\lambda\right)\mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2}\lambda\mathbf{b}$, where $\lambda$ is a scalar constant. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q10|b|ms: (b) M1: Uses $\overrightarrow{ON} = \overrightarrow{OC} + \lambda\overrightarrow{CM}$. A1*: Correct proof, substituting $\overrightarrow{OC} = 2\mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{CM} = -\frac{3}{2}\mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}$, to obtain $\overrightarrow{ON} = \left(2 - \frac{3}{2}\lambda\right)\mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2}\lambda\mathbf{b}$. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q10|c|ms: (c) M1: Deduces [editor: since $N$ lies on $OB$, so $\overrightarrow{ON}$ has no component of $\mathbf{a}$] that $2 - \frac{3}{2}\lambda = 0$, and solves to find $\lambda = \frac{4}{3}$. A1*: Substitutes back to get $\overrightarrow{ON} = \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{b}$, so $\overrightarrow{NB} = \overrightarrow{OB} - \overrightarrow{ON} = \mathbf{b} - \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{b} = \frac{1}{3}\mathbf{b}$, hence $ON : NB = \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{b} : \frac{1}{3}\mathbf{b} = 2 : 1$. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|stem: Figure 8 shows a sketch of the curve $C$ with equation $y = x^x, \; x > 0$.
units.P2_June2019_Q11|a|text: (a) Find, by firstly taking logarithms, the $x$ coordinate of the turning point of $C$. (Solutions based entirely on graphical or numerical methods are not acceptable.) (5 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|a|ms: (a) B1: Takes logs of both sides: $\ln y = x\ln x$ (condone use of log base $10$, or writing $y = e^{x\ln x}$). M1: Differentiates implicitly: $\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$ (or, using $y = e^{x\ln x}$, $\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(\ln x + \frac{x}{x}\right)e^{x\ln x}$). A1: Correct differentiated equation, e.g. $\frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$, or $\frac{dy}{dx} = x^x(1 + \ln x)$. M1: Sets $1 + \ln x = 0$ and rearranges to make $\ln x = k$ ($k$ a constant, $k < 0$), then $x = \ldots$ . A1: $x = e^{-1}$, or awrt $0.368$ only (with no other solutions given). (5 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|b|text:
The point $P(\alpha, 2)$ lies on $C$.
(b) Show that $1.5 < \alpha < 1.6$ (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|b|ms: (b) M1: Attempts both $1.5^{1.5}$ ($=$ awrt $1.8$) and $1.6^{1.6}$ ($=$ awrt $2.1$), with at least one result correct to 1 dp. A1: $1.8\ldots < 2$ and $2.1\ldots > 2$, and since $C$ is continuous, there is a sign change between $x=1.5$ and $x=1.6$, so $1.5 < \alpha < 1.6$. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|c|text:
A possible iteration formula that could be used in an attempt to find $\alpha$ is
$x_{n+1} = 2x_n^{1 - x_n}$
Using this formula with $x_1 = 1.5$,
(c) find $x_4$ to 3 decimal places, (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|c|ms: (c) M1: Attempts $x_{n+1} = 2x_n^{1-x_n}$ at least once with $x_1 = 1.5$ (can be implied by $2(1.5)^{1-1.5} =$ awrt $1.63$). A1: $x_4 = 1.673$ (3 dp), cao (via $x_2 = 1.63299\ldots$, $x_3 = 1.46626\ldots$, $x_4 = 1.67313\ldots$). (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|d|text: (d) describe the long-term behaviour of $x_n$ (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q11|d|ms: (d) B1: States that the sequence oscillates / is periodic / non-convergent / divergent / fluctuates / alternates (e.g. $1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, \ldots$). B1: States that it oscillates specifically between $1$ and $2$, or is periodic with period $2$. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q12|a|ms: (a) M1: Correct valid method forming a common denominator of $\sin\theta\cos\theta$, i.e. $\frac{\cos 3\theta\cos\theta + \sin 3\theta\sin\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}$ (or, equivalently, starting from the RHS and expanding $\cos 2\theta$ as $\cos 3\theta\cos\theta + \sin 3\theta\sin\theta$). A1: Proceeds to show that the numerator simplifies to $\cos(3\theta-\theta) = \cos 2\theta$, using the compound-angle formula for cosine. dM1: Applies a correct $\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ to the denominator, dependent on the previous M mark. A1*: Correct proof: $\frac{\cos 2\theta}{\frac{1}{2}\sin 2\theta} = 2\cot 2\theta$. (4 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q12|b|text:
(b) Hence solve, for $90^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ$, the equation
$\frac{\cos 3\theta}{\sin\theta} + \frac{\sin 3\theta}{\cos\theta} = 4$
giving any solutions to one decimal place. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q12|b|ms: (b) M1: Evidence of applying $\cot 2\theta = \frac{1}{\tan 2\theta}$ to rewrite the equation as $\tan 2\theta = \frac{1}{2}$ (o.e., $k \neq 0$). dM1: Rearranges to give $\tan 2\theta = k$, $k \neq 0$, and applies $\arctan k$; dependent on the previous M mark. A1: Uses $90 \leqslant \theta \leqslant 180$ to deduce the only solution $\theta =$ awrt $103.3$ (1 dp), with no other (extraneous) solutions given. (3 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q13|stem: A manufacturer produces a storage tank modelled as a hollow circular cylinder, closed at one end, with a hemispherical shell at the other end (Figure 9). The walls are assumed to have negligible thickness. The cylinder has radius $r$ metres and height $h$ metres; the hemisphere has radius $r$ metres. The volume of the tank is $6 \text{ m}^3$. [A sphere of radius $r$ has volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ and surface area $4\pi r^2$.]
units.P2_June2019_Q13|a|text: (a) Show that, according to the model, the surface area of the tank, in $\text{m}^2$, is given by $A = \frac{12}{r} + \frac{5}{3}\pi r^2$. (4 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q13|a|ms: (a) B1: correct expression for the volume of the tank in terms of $r$ and $h$ (cylinder + hemisphere). M1: complete process of substituting their $h$ (in terms of $r$) into an expression for the surface area of the form $A = \alpha r^2 + \beta rh$. A1: correct simplified or unsimplified surface area expression, e.g. $A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r\left(\frac{6}{\pi r^2} - \frac{2}{3}r\right) + \pi r^2$. A1*: proceeds, with rigorous and careful reasoning, to $A = \frac{12}{r} + \frac{5}{3}\pi r^2$ (given answer). (4 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q13|b|text: The manufacturer needs to minimise the surface area of the tank. (b) Use calculus to find the radius of the tank for which the surface area is a minimum. (4 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q13|b|ms: (b) M1: uses the model and differentiates $\frac{\lambda}{r} + \mu r^2$ to give $\alpha r^{-2} + \beta r$; $\lambda, \mu, \alpha, \beta \neq 0$. A1: correct $\frac{dA}{dr} = -\frac{12}{r^2} + \frac{10}{3}\pi r$. M1: sets their $\frac{dA}{dr} = 0$ and rearranges to $r^3 = k$ for some constant $k$. A1: $r =$ awrt $1.05$ (m), or exact form. (4 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q13|c|text: (c) Calculate the minimum surface area of the tank, giving your answer to the nearest integer. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q13|c|ms: (c) M1: substitutes their $r$ back into the expression for $A$. A1ft: $A = 17$ ($\text{m}^2$) or awrt $17$ ($\text{m}^2$) (ft only for $0.6 \leqslant$ their $r \leqslant 1.3$ found from $\frac{dA}{dr} = 0$ in (b)). (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q14|a|text:
(a) Use the substitution $u = 4 - \sqrt{h}$ to show that
$\int \frac{dh}{4 - \sqrt{h}} = -8\ln|4 - \sqrt{h}| - 2\sqrt{h} + k$
where $k$ is a constant (6 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q14|a|ms:
(a) B1: States or uses $ rac{du}{dh} = - rac{1}{2\sqrt{h}}$ [editor: (equivalently, since $u=4-\sqrt{h}$ gives $\sqrt{h}=4-u$ and $h=(4-u)^2$, $ rac{dh}{du} = -2(4-u)$)]. M1: Complete method for applying $u=4-\sqrt{h}$ to $ rac{dh}{4-\sqrt{h}}$ to give an expression of the form $ rac{k(4-u)}{u} \, \{du\}$, $k

units.P2_June2019_Q14|b|text:
A team of scientists is studying a species of slow growing tree. The rate of change in height of a tree in this species is modelled by the differential equation
$\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{t^{0.25}(4 - \sqrt{h})}{20}$
where $h$ is the height in metres and $t$ is the time, measured in years, after the tree is planted.
(b) Find, according to the model, the range in heights of trees in this species. (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q14|b|ms: (b) M1: Uses the context of the model, understanding that the tree keeps growing until $\frac{dh}{dt} = 0$, i.e. $4 - \sqrt{h} = 0$. A1: Deduces $0 \leqslant h < 16$ (or $h \leqslant 16$, or an equivalent statement giving $16$ as the limiting height). (2 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q14|c|text:
One of these trees is one metre high when it is first planted. According to the model,
(c) calculate the time this tree would take to reach a height of $12$ metres, giving your answer to 3 significant figures. (7 marks)
units.P2_June2019_Q14|c|ms: (c) B1: Separates the variables correctly: $\frac{dh}{4-\sqrt{h}} = \frac{t^{0.25}}{20} \, dt$ ($dh$ and $dt$ in the correct positions; can be implied by later working). M1: Integrates $t^{0.25}$ to give $\lambda t^{1.25}$, $\lambda \neq 0$. A1: Correct integration, e.g. $-8\ln|4-\sqrt{h}| - 2\sqrt{h} = \frac{1}{25}t^{1.25} \; \{+ \text{constant}\}$ (or $20(-8\ln|4-\sqrt{h}| - 2\sqrt{h}) = \frac{4}{5}t^{1.25}$). M1: Some evidence of applying both $t=0$, $h=1$ to their model (containing a constant of integration) to find that constant, OR applying limits $h=1$ to $h=12$ and $t=0$ to $T$ and subtracting. dM1: Complete process of finding the constant of integration (or applying both sets of limits), then applying $h=12$ to give an equation in $t$ only; dependent on the previous M mark. M1: Rearranges their equation to make $t^{1.25} = \ldots$, then $t = \ldots$ ($t>0$), using a correct method. A1: $t =$ awrt $75.2$ (years) (3 sf). (7 marks)
